Over the past 3 years, Kyrgyzstan has managed to ensure annual economic growth of 9%, with GDP per capita increasing by 1.7 times, which reflects both post-crisis recovery and the progress in structural transformation. Employment remains a national priority. The government has adopted targeted programs to accelerate the transition from informal to formal employment, foster entrepreneurship, expand access to vocational training, and enhance youth employment. The share of youth not in education, employment, or training declined to 18.6% in 2023, though there is a substantial gender gap. To improve the quality of employment, The new labor code has been adopted along with reforms in wage policy and the introduction of decent work standards and zero injury approach. Improvements have been made in labor statistics with increased attention to accounting for migration flows. The child labor rate decreased to 19.6% in 2010. The Kyrgyz Republic emphasizes the importance of targeted reforms to support vulnerable groups, including women, youth, migrants, and persons with disabilities. We remain committed to advancing an inclusive, sustainable, and rights-based labor market in line with international labor standards.
I thank the representative of Kyrgyzstan. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of South Africa, to be followed by UNDRR. South Africa, you have the floor.

Distinguished Vice President, Moderator, and panelists, over the next 10 years, an unprecedented 1.2 billion young people in the Global South will become working-age adults, and they will need and jobs. Despite economic growth in many of our countries, many of our economies failed to create sufficient job opportunities for those who are able and willing to work, indicating that economic growth on its own is not enough to solve the missing jobs crisis. Where jobs are created, they are often not transformative. They do not bring with them the required level of wages, social protection, security, and dignity. Necessary for decent work. Developing countries' reliance on commodity exports and the limited opportunities to climb global value chains in part underpin this poor jobs performance. To address these challenges, South Africa has created a task force on inclusive economic growth, industrialization, employment, and reduced inequality to prioritize decent jobs. under its G20 presidency. This task force will deliver a set of G20 principles to try and address high informality, limited access to quality education, and weak labor market institutions, policy and regulatory reforms, digital transformation, and migration, and to address the opportunities of the green transition and digital transitions. We support the implementation of Compromiso de Sevilla, UNOC III, and the Pact of the Future. And I thank you, Chair.
Now, thank you, South Africa— representative of South Africa. Now I give the floor to distinguished representative of Spain, to be followed by Honduras.

Thank you. Spain is fully committed to inclusive and sustainable economic development and to decent employment for all. At the national level, unemployment rate has fallen in the last 10 years to 10%, which is the best figure in the last 17 years. The number of unemployed women is the lowest ever. Thanks to the 2021 labor reform, we've reduced temporary contracts. In addition, the increase in minimum wage of €61 since 2018 has made it possible to reduce inequalities, the risk of poverty and exclusion, especially for women. Decent work is the central axis of Spain's labour policy. Thanks to the introduction of paid leave in the event of extreme weather conditions or natural disasters and the introduction of the obligation for companies with more than 50 workers to have equality and prevention plans to prevent harassment against LGBTI staff, We have promoted measures for the incorporation of the labor market of young people, people with disabilities, and to enhance long-term employment, improving professional training, promoting work-life balance. In the future, we're working hard to improve conditions in the care sector. We will reduce the average working day to 37.5 hours per week and update legislation on occupational risks. Our system highlights social protections. Spanish cooperation has supported the Global Accelerator for Social Protection and Decent Work promoted by the UNSG. We've also made financial contributions to this and other initiatives to promote joint and coordinated work with the UN system and IFIs to achieve this goal. We're working with the ILO on the action plan for transition from the informal to the formal economy. Finally, we're working for the effective formalization of employment in all countries and for universal social protections and decent work, as we said at FFD4 in Seville. Spain will continue to support those countries that commit to increasing their investments in social protection by 2% per year. Thank you.

You have the floor. Thank you, Chair, Excellencies. Distinguished delegates, colleagues, and partners, as we enter the final stretch of the 2030 Agenda, the urgency to safeguard decent work and economic growth has never been greater. This was reaffirmed at the 4th International Conference on Financing for Development in Sevilla, where member states emphasized investment in disaster risk reduction and resilience to protect and sustain economic progress. Disasters are eroding economic resilience, causing job losses, business closures, and productivity declines. According to the 2025 Global Assessment Report on Disaster Risk Reduction, Annual direct losses from disasters now exceed $202 billion, with total losses including cascading and ecosystem impacts exceeding $2.3 trillion. Excellencies, disaster risk reduction strategies must be integrated into employment, labor, and social protection policies to build resilient livelihoods. To achieve SDG 8, We must embed risk-informed strategies into economic planning and investment. Disaster risk reduction is more than a shield. It is a catalyst for inclusive, sustainable growth. It protects existing jobs and creates new ones in resilience-building sectors. At the Global Platform last month, Member States endorsed the Geneva Call for Disaster Risk Reduction, outlining 8 priority actions to strengthen economic resilience and to protect livelihoods. We must act with a sense of urgency. Investing in DRR means investing in economic stability, productivity, and decent work. The International Labour Organization estimates that 20% of the world's population is committed to volunteering actions, whether formal or informal. This number represents the the strength of this movement that's often underestimated. Volunteers often act in the field day to day. I'm thinking of Valentine, who works in Senegal, who is helping to support the Women and Shells program aiming to improve working conditions of women in mangroves. I'm thinking of Vivian as well in Burkina Faso and Togo, who is working at the SAR Afrique NGO to promote youth employment. These examples illustrate the contribution of international volunteering to sustainable economic models based in specific countries. Therefore, we believe it's important now to strengthen recognition of volunteering as a tool for economic and social transformation and to help to make it more visible. We also need to incorporate volunteering on the political level.
I thank the representative of France. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Guatemala, to be followed by Ecuador. Guatemala, you have the floor.

Excellencies, distinguished delegations, yesterday we talked about how to connect the drivers of our economy with the aspirations of our people. There's a high level of informality where the majority of Guatemalans work without social protections and without full labor rights. This is the story of one of the greatest gender gaps in history and also the vast number of young people who are not studying or in work. And this is the problem we have decided to tackle. In order not to try and do so blindly, we have taken a fundamental technical step. We are transforming our employment survey system to design public policies to be surgical in our precision. This intelligence is feeding our overall government policy through 2028 that is driving a humane economy. We're not talking about an assistance or benefit economy. We're talking about empowerment. In order to support our economy, we have scholarships for the future as well as technical training and university. We have selected more than 1,500 people already. We are going for the heart of our economy, SMEs, and facilitating their access to credit and training, enhancing the participation of young people and women in enhancing their skills for the future. Excellencies, Guatemala does not aspire to growth that leaves half of its population behind. We are aspiring to development where each Guatemalan person can build a life project with certainty and dignity. I thank you.

I thank the representative of Ecuador and now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Sovereign Order of Malta, to be followed by Switzerland.

Mr. President, distinguished colleagues, it is an honor to address this Assembly on Sustainable Development Goal 8, Decent Work and Economic growth and its vital role in advancing the 2030 Agenda. As the Permanent Observer of the Sovereign Order of Malta, a lay religious order with over 900 years of service to the sick and the poor, I bring a faith-based perspective. Work is not just economic output but a source of dignity, purpose, and service to the common good. Across 120 countries, the Order's humanitarian work from hospitals to livelihood programs, affirms that economic growth must be rooted in human dignity. In February, our mission to the UN hosted an interfaith conference on the ethical issues of artificial intelligence. Professor John Tasioulas of Oxford University reminded us that AI's trajectory is not inevitable. It reflects human choices which must promote dignity. He warned that as AI automates work, we risk losing the meaning, skill, and cooperation that work brings. Financial compensation alone cannot replace the fulfillment people find in contributing to something larger than themselves. As Pope Francis said, what gives dignity is work. Decent work means being part of society in a way that matters. Mr. President, the COVID-19 pandemic created a dramatic and lasting awareness of mental health challenges, challenges that have not disappeared. The prolonged isolation, the widespread reduction in daily personal interaction, and the sudden disruption of work life exposed vulnerabilities in our societies that are— that we are still grappling with. These issues remind us how deeply human beings need connection, structure, and a sense of purpose. As we advance towards the 2030 Agenda, let us reaffirm that decent work is not only about economic output but about purpose. Thank you very much.

I thank the representative of Switzerland. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Costa Rica, to be followed by Azerbaijan. Costa Rica, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. To achieve economic growth that is truly inclusive and sustainable, We must radically transform our development— economic development paradigms. First, sustainability and equity must be endogenous variables, not externalities in our growth models. Economies that degrade natural capital and exclude population sectors inevitably face structural limits to their growth. Costa Rica advocates for policies that internalize environmental and social costs, ensuring effective inclusion of the most vulnerable. Second, technological innovation and human capital are fundamental multipliers of inclusive growth. To close access gaps that disproportionately affect women and youth, it is imperative that we invest in technical education, digital skills, and the care economy. We must mobilize both domestic and international resources and establish strategic partnerships across governments, the private sector, and civil society to optimize capital allocation to towards productive and sustainable investments. Mr. President, Bangladesh reaffirms that decent work and economic growth is not a standalone objective. Over 80% of our workforce remains in the informal sector, making the formalization of work, skills development, and entrepreneurship not just economic imperatives but essential for delivering on SDGs 1, 5, 9, and 10. Our interim government's reform agenda prioritizes the formalization of the informal sector, enhanced labor protections, SME support, and youth employment, all essential to fostering equitable growth and leaving no one behind. We are investing in inclusive growth. The Skills for Employment Investment Program has trained 700,000 youth with a 60% job placement rate. Over 41,000 women have received business grants through urban livelihood programs. But numbers alone do not capture the full story. To truly transform development, we must rethink the way we build economies. This is where the concept of social business, pioneered by Nobel Peace Laureate Professor Muhammad Yunus, plays a groundbreaking role. These non-dividend sustainable enterprises reinvest all profits to solve social problems, creating jobs, restoring dignity, and uplifting communities. In a world facing polycrisis, we believe the social business model offers a resilient, inclusive, and locally rooted solution that links SDG 8 with health, education, gender equality, and innovation. As Bangladesh transitions from LDC status in 2026, we are calling for international cooperation to integrate social business and blended finance into SDG investment frameworks, especially for SMEs and youth-led enterprises. We also urge greater attention to ESG accountability climate-resilient jobs, and digital inclusion, especially for rural populations. Thank you.

The growth— this growth was driven by strong domestic demand, higher investments, and a rebound in exports. The unemployment rate dropped to 3.2%, and the labor force participation rate rose to 70.6%. showing good progress. We, for example, need various data on youth employment and labor rights for evidence-based policies and to monitor progress. Furthermore, as the caste system has impacted people globally all too long, we demand on the launch of a dedicated UN Forum on Communities Discriminated on Work and Descent to finally address the systemic marginalization of 270 million people facing caste and descent-based discrimination. Finally, we request broad implementation of tax exemptions and subsidies for those paying and hiring youth, prioritizing marginalized groups to promote decent living and sustainable employment, and call for expanded access to informal technical and vocational education training programs.

Now, I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Suriname, to be followed by Indonesia. Suriname, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, distinguished delegates. Suriname recognizes that sustained inclusive economic growth and decent work for all are at the heart of the 2030 Agenda. With only 5 years left, SDG 8 remains one of the most off-track goals, yet it is the foundation for reducing poverty, advancing gender equality, education, and building climate resilience. Suriname continues to face significant challenges. Unemployment remains too high, especially among the poor and in our interior regions. Informality is growing, leaving many workers without protection or stable income. Workplace safety still needs urgent improvements, and we face gaps in reliable labor markets data that weaken planning and action. Our response is guided by our multiannual development plan, our Decent Work Country Program, and our labor market policy. These plans aim to diversify our economy and create more secure jobs supported by new laws and funds like our Production Credit Fund and the Savings and Stabilization Fund. To tackle informality and unlock more decent jobs, Suriname is expanding training and entrepreneurship support. We have supported over 637 small and medium businesses since 2023, with special focus on women and indigenous entrepreneurs. We reach people in all regions with free skills training and job placement support through our Training for Employment Roadmap and institutions like the Suriname Hospitality and Tourism Training Center. We must strengthen institutions, close data gaps, and reach all communities, and we call on our partners to keep supporting Suriname with capacity building, technology, and innovative financing for social protection.
I thank the representative of Suriname. I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia, to be followed by Gambia. Indonesia, you are—

To prepare the workforce for the green economic shifts, it needs to outline strategic actions to strengthen skill development, promote inclusive and sustainable employment, and create quality green jobs in the renewables energy. To promote inclusive employment Indonesia is expanding access to childcare, ensuring equal pay, and encouraging women's participation in formal sectors. The government is also advancing social inclusion for persons with disabilities through the establishment of disability service units and for older persons through the National Aging Strategy. Indonesia stands ready to share the skill and scale these approaches and to collaborate with global partners. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Indonesia. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Gambia, to be followed by Malawi. Gambia, you have the floor.

Our takeaway for call for action from this meeting, Chairperson, is we want to strengthen partnership We also want to insist that the access to concessional financing and technology is very important for smaller countries like ours to achieve our goal. At the meantime, we'll be working towards creating a favorable work environment for our youth. I thank you, Chairperson.
I thank the representative of Malawi. Now, I give the floor to the distinguished representative United Nations University, to be followed by Ireland. UNU, you have the floor.

Thank you, Mr.

Chair. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, we know decent work and employment are central to reducing poverty and inequalities and promoting inclusive, sustainable, country-led growth. We are on the heels of the 4th International Conference on Financing for Development and moving to implementation of the Compromiso de Sevilla. It is important to connect the jobs agenda to mobilizing domestic revenues and fiscal space, recognizing the criticality of decent work in growing the tax base and increasing productivity. In part, more effort must be made to expand earnings and employment through supporting micro and small enterprises and supply chains, including through formalization, as most of the world's workers and enterprises remain in the informal economy where pay and working conditions can be meager. More attention should also be paid to generating demographic dividends by increasing the human capital and workforce participation of women and youth, as well as older people who want to remain in work.

This includes taking an age-based approach to AI, digital policies, and employment to ensure intergenerational opportunities are optimized.

The global gap between men and women in employment is 24% and tends to be even higher in parts of the Global South. In the Middle East and North Africa, for example, female labor force participation is under 25— 20%, while it's over 70% for men, with clear links to SDG 5, improving access to care, laws, education, and technology should be prioritized.

Among youth worldwide, some 20% are not in education, employment, or training and struggle to secure decent work or start a business due to inadequate job creation, skills mismatches, or lack of credit mobility, among other challenges.

An estimated 1.2 billion young people are set to enter the labor force in low- and middle-income economies over the next decade, and just 400 million jobs are due to be created. This math means policies must engage and ensure private sector viability and accelerate sectors strategically.

Countries can also see sizable economic gains from the so-called silver economy, the work and purchasing power of those over the age of 50.

This requires investments in health and longevity, SDG 3, along with reskilling, financial inclusion, and business operations support. Finally, let's remember—

Thank you, Chair. Ireland aligns itself with the statement of the European Union and has the following to add in national capacity. Decent work and economic growth are at the core of sustainable development and the well-being of individuals. Ireland recognizes that social protection is critical to address income inequality and the persistent exclusion of the poorest from the benefits of economic growth. Investing in people goes hand in hand with increasing competitiveness, competitiveness, and reducing inequalities. Ireland's policy for international development, A Better World, commits to promoting inclusive economic growth and trade, to support initiatives that seek foster trade and investment as well as helping developing countries build their domestic and international trade capacity and infrastructure to ensure that they can access the economic benefits of expanded regional and global trade opportunities. The 2nd World Summit for Social Development is set to take place in November 2025, and renewing the Global Social Contract is key to rebuilding trust, social cohesion, and solidarity with ongoing challenges posed by demographic decarbonization and digital transitions. The need to align investments in education, vocational training, lifelong education and skills development so that workers' competencies respond to labor market opportunities and support fair, sustainable, and just transition of our economies.
